name: Newton's plague years and the Principia
scope: The eighteen months that rebuilt physics, and the apple story told honestly. T1: in 1665 plague closed Cambridge and sent a 22-year-old undergraduate home to a Lincolnshire farm, Woolsthorpe Manor; in roughly eighteen months there Isaac Newton invented his calculus of fluxions, split white light with a prism, and began on gravity (the hook: the most productive stretch in the history of science happened in a lockdown). T2: the apple, told as what it actually is -- Newton's OWN late anecdote, related over tea in a Kensington garden on 15 April 1726 when he was 83, written down by William Stukeley and published in his 1752 Memoirs; the apple fell BESIDE him and never touched his head, and the question he said it provoked was why an apple always falls straight down toward the Earth's centre. T3: what he did with the thought -- the 'moon test': he compared the force needed to hold the Moon in her orbit with the strength of gravity at the Earth's surface and, in his own words, found them 'answer pretty nearly'; the Moon is falling too, it just keeps missing. T4: the visit that forced the book -- in August 1684 Edmond Halley rode to Cambridge and asked what path a planet would take under an inverse-square force; Newton answered at once that it would be an ellipse, said he had calculated it years before, and could not find the paper. Halley pushed him to write it up and paid for the printing of the Principia (1687) out of his own pocket. T5: the priority fight with Robert Hooke, who had proposed the inverse-square idea in letters around 1679-80 and demanded credit -- Newton's substantive answer was that guessing a rule is not the same as PROVING it produces the observed orbits; the distinction between a hunch and a derivation that predicts is the rung's real content. Further rungs: the unification itself (before Newton, heaven and Earth obeyed different laws; after him one law governs apple, Moon, tide and comet); and the honest complication that Newton left more manuscript pages on alchemy and biblical chronology than on physics.
source: Grokipedia, 'Isaac Newton' (read directly via browser; grokipedia.com returns 403 to plain fetch) -- annus mirabilis 1665-66 at Woolsthorpe, fluxions, prism work, Hooke correspondence Dec 1679 and the priority dispute, alchemy/theology manuscripts exceeding scientific output. Wikipedia, 'Edmond Halley' -- the August 1684 Cambridge visit, Halley funding and publishing the Principia at his own expense. Royal Society facsimile of William Stukeley, 'Memoirs of Sir Isaac Newton's Life' (1752), recording the 15 April 1726 Kensington garden conversation. Newton's own recollection of the moon test ('found them answer pretty nearly'), quoted from his memorandum in standard Newton scholarship.
framing_note: Voice: DISCOVERY, with the famous myth told AS a myth -- which is on-voice gold here, not a caveat. Accuracy rail (the one that matters): the apple did NOT hit his head, and the story is Newton's own telling in old age, recorded by Stukeley; the bank presents it as a documented late anecdote of uncertain embellishment -- never as fiction, never as eyewitness fact. Secondary rail: Newton used a poor value for the Earth's radius in 1666, which is why the moon test only 'answered pretty nearly' -- say 'roughly agreed', not 'confirmed'. Dinner-test payoff: T2 (the kid gets to correct every cartoon they have ever seen). Distractor mine: Descartes' vortices (the reigning respectable rival), Hooke, Christopher Wren, Halley, Kepler's laws as description-without-cause, Leibniz on calculus -- all real adjacent claimants and real adjacent theories, never joke options. Anti-restatement: the T3 stem describes the SCENE (a young man on a farm comparing two numbers) and must never say 'inverse-square law' before the answer names it. Lane border: the Great Plague itself belongs to HISTORY -- Woolsthorpe appears only as the workplace.
history_overlap: history bank: the Great Plague of London (1665-66) and the closure of Cambridge -- science keeps Woolsthorpe purely as Newton's workplace and builds no plague-epidemiology or London-social rung. philosophy bank may hold Newton and Leibniz as figures -- keep the calculus dispute to a single credit rung, no metaphysics of the infinitesimal.

name: Galileo's ramps: the falling-bodies experiment he actually did
scope: The apocryphal drop, the real experiment, and the demonstration that finally ran in a vacuum. T1: Galileo could not time a falling rock -- nothing in 1600 ticked fast enough -- so he DILUTED gravity: he cut a straight groove down a wooden beam about twelve cubits long, lined it with smooth parchment, propped one end up, and rolled a hard bronze ball down it (the answer is the ramp, the inclined plane). T2: the clock he built for it -- a big vessel of water with a thin pipe at the bottom; he caught the jet in a glass during each descent and WEIGHED the water afterwards, because ratios of weights are ratios of times. T3: the result -- in successive equal ticks the ball covers distances in the ratio 1, 3, 5, 7...; total distance grows as the SQUARE of the elapsed time, and the ratio is the same whatever the ball's weight. T4: the Leaning Tower drop is probably apocryphal -- the sole source is Vincenzo Viviani, Galileo's last student, in a life written in 1654 and published in 1717, and Galileo himself never mentions it; meanwhile a genuinely documented drop test HAD been run, by Simon Stevin and Jan Cornets de Groot at Delft around 1586, lead balls from about thirty feet, reporting that the lighter ball landed essentially with the heavier. T5: the argument that needs no apparatus at all -- Galileo's thought experiment in Two New Sciences (1638): tie a heavy ball to a light one; if light things fall slower the light one must drag on the heavy one and slow it, yet the pair is heavier than either and so should fall fastest of all. Aristotle's rule breaks on pure logic before anyone drops anything. Further rungs: the vindication -- on 2 August 1971 Apollo 15 commander David Scott dropped a 1.32 kg aluminium geology hammer and a 0.03 kg falcon feather on the airless Moon on live television, and they struck the surface together; the young Galileo timing a swinging lamp in Pisa Cathedral against his own PULSE and noticing the swing takes the same time whether wide or narrow (Viviani's story again -- the lamp on display today was hung in 1587, after the date claimed, so the specific lamp is wrong even if the observation is his); and the kid-replicable version tonight, a marble on a tilted board with a phone stopwatch, or a sheet of paper laid flat on top of a book and dropped.
source: Wikipedia, 'Galileo's Leaning Tower of Pisa experiment' -- Viviani as sole source, historians' doubt, Stevin and de Groot at Delft c.1586, Philoponus and Benedetti as earlier dissenters. Wikipedia, 'Two New Sciences' -- the twelve-cubit grooved beam, parchment lining, bronze ball, the water-vessel clock and weighing method. Wikipedia, 'Equations for a falling body' -- the odd-number rule 1,3,5,7 and distance proportional to time squared. NASA Science, 'The Apollo 15 Hammer-Feather Drop' and NSSDC lunar page -- 2 August 1971, David Scott, 1.32 kg hammer and 0.03 kg falcon feather, released from about 1.6 m, striking together. Museo Galileo / Antonio Favaro on the Pisa Cathedral lamp: the present lamp postdates Galileo's stay, so Viviani's lamp is legend; a period votive lamp survives in the Aulla Chapel. Grokipedia consulted for Galileo biography.
framing_note: Voice: DISCOVERY + the test-it-yourself soul -- this is the single most kid-replicable ladder in the sub-strand and every rung should feel like an invitation. Accuracy rail (the one that matters): the Tower drop is Viviani's late claim, NOT Galileo's; the ramps and the water clock ARE documented in Two New Sciences. No rung may assert the Pisa drop as fact, and the Stevin/de Groot rung is the honest credit that replaces it. Secondary rail: if any rung wants to quote Galileo repeating the run 'a full hundred times', verify against the Crew and de Salvio translation before shipping -- otherwise say only that he repeated it many times with no appreciable discrepancy. Dinner-test payoff: T4 (the most famous physics experiment in history probably never happened, and someone else did the real one first). Distractor mine: Aristotle's rule that fall speed goes with weight, medieval impetus theory, John Philoponus, Giambattista Benedetti, air resistance mistaken for the whole story -- all live positions serious thinkers held. Anti-restatement: the T3 stem gives the SETUP (ball, ramp, equal ticks) and must never contain 'squares' or 'accelerates uniformly' before the answer supplies it.
history_overlap: philosophy bank: Aristotle as a figure -- this ladder keys only the TEST that broke Aristotle's physics, never his metaphysics, logic or ethics. history bank may carry Apollo 15 as a mission -- the hammer-feather rung keys the Galileo demonstration and the airless surface, not the mission narrative or the space race.

name: Tycho's data and the eight arcminutes Kepler refused to fudge
scope: The ladder that teaches that the residual IS the discovery. T1: a Danish nobleman given his own island, Hven, built a palace-observatory called Uraniborg and spent twenty years measuring star and planet positions with giant quadrants and sextants and NO telescope -- it had not been invented -- reaching an accuracy approaching one arcminute, roughly five times better than anyone before him: Tycho Brahe. T2: the nose, as a de-myth rung -- he lost the bridge of his nose in a midnight sword duel with his cousin Manderup Parsberg on 29 December 1566 after a drunken quarrel over a point of mathematics, and wore a metal prosthesis for the rest of his life; legend made it silver and gold, but chemical analysis of his exhumed remains (reported 2012) found the traces were BRASS. T3: the handoff -- Tycho died in 1601 and his assistant Johannes Kepler inherited the observations, after a fight with Tycho's heirs, and was set the hardest target: Mars. T4: THE PAYOFF -- after roughly eight years Kepler had a circular model (his 'vicarious hypothesis') that reproduced Tycho's positions to about two arcminutes, except for a stubborn residue of EIGHT arcminutes, about a quarter of the Moon's apparent width, a discrepancy invisible to any eye but Tycho's. He could have shrugged. Instead he wrote in Astronomia Nova that because they could not be disregarded, these eight minutes alone would lead the way to reforming the whole of astronomy -- and he threw out the circle. T5: what replaced it -- the ellipse with the Sun at one focus, plus the equal-areas law, so a planet must move FASTER when it is nearer the Sun; published in Astronomia Nova (1609), ending two thousand years in which the heavens were assumed to move in circles. Further rungs: the third law (the square of a planet's period tracks the cube of its distance) in Harmonices Mundi (1619), the rule Newton would later DERIVE from gravity and Halley would use to catch a comet; and the human rung -- in the middle of this work Kepler abandoned his post to lead the legal defence of his mother Katharina, imprisoned in August 1620 on 49 counts of witchcraft and freed in the autumn of 1621, having refused to confess even when brought before the tribunal and threatened with torture.
source: Grokipedia, 'Johannes Kepler' (read directly via browser) -- Tycho's opposition observations of Mars 1582-1600 accurate to about 1 arcminute, the eight-year Mars analysis, Astronomia Nova 1609 and the first two laws, the third law in Harmonices Mundi 1619, the heirs' dispute over the data, Katharina's witchcraft accusation. Wikipedia, 'Astronomia nova' -- the eight-arcminute residual against the vicarious hypothesis and Kepler's documented statement that these eight minutes alone would lead the way to reforming the whole of astronomy. Wikipedia, 'Tycho Brahe' -- the 29 December 1566 duel with Manderup Parsberg, the 2012 chemical analysis finding brass rather than silver or gold, Uraniborg, accuracy approaching one arcminute. American Physical Society, 'August 1620: Kepler's Mother Imprisoned for Witchcraft', and Wikipedia, 'Katharina Kepler'.
framing_note: Voice: DISCOVERY with the sub-strand's deepest method lesson -- a small number that will not go away is the most valuable object in science. Accuracy rail (the one that matters): the nose was BRASS on modern analysis, not silver -- the silver version must be told explicitly AS the legend, and the stem should carry the duel-over-a-maths-argument hook so the answer carries the metal. Secondary rail: Kepler's eight-minutes line is a documented passage in Astronomia Nova -- quote it as documented or paraphrase plainly; do not sharpen it into a slogan he never wrote. Dinner-test payoff: T4 (a quarter of a Moon-width of error rewrote the solar system). Distractor mine: epicycles, the equant, Ptolemy's system, Copernicus's own circles, and Tycho's geo-heliocentric compromise -- every one a model a serious astronomer defended, which is exactly the point. Anti-restatement: the T4 stem describes what Kepler SAW (a model that fits everything except a sliver) and must never name the ellipse before the answer does. Invert the wonder: put 'eight arcminutes' in the stem as the astonishing smallness, make what he DID with it the answer.
history_overlap: history bank: European witch trials as a phenomenon -- the Katharina Kepler rung keys Johannes's personal legal defence and the years it cost his astronomy, never the witch-hunt as a social episode. geography bank may tour Hven as a place -- Uraniborg appears here only as the instrument platform.

name: Halley's comet: a prediction tested from beyond the grave
scope: The first great successful prediction of a future event by physical theory. T1: in 1705 an English astronomer studying old comet records noticed that three apparitions -- 1531, 1607 and 1682 -- traced nearly the same orbit, and concluded they were not three comets but ONE comet on a loop of about seventy-six years, due back around 1758: Edmond Halley. T2: the hook -- Halley was born in 1656 and knew perfectly well he would be dead before the test; he wrote that if it did return as he said, posterity should acknowledge that this was first found out by an Englishman. He died in January 1742, sixteen years short. T3: the refinement -- Alexis Clairaut, Joseph Lalande and Nicole-Reine Lepaute spent months of hand computation working out how the gravity of Jupiter and Saturn would DELAY the comet, and published a predicted perihelion of about mid-April 1759 with roughly a month's stated uncertainty; Lepaute did an enormous share of the arithmetic. T4: the vindication -- on Christmas night, 25 December 1758, it was a German farmer and amateur astronomer, Johann Georg Palitzsch, who spotted it first; perihelion came on 13 March 1759, Jupiter and Saturn having held it back by 618 days exactly as Newton's law required. T5: what it changed -- before this, comets were omens, portents and (for Aristotle) burning exhalations in the upper air; after it, a comet's return was a date you could write down and check. Newton's law had now predicted something nobody had ever seen. Further rungs: Tycho Brahe had already shown by parallax that a comet lies far beyond the Moon, killing the atmospheric theory; and the standing invitation -- the comet returned in 1835, 1910 and 1986 and is due again in 2061, which is a date a ten-year-old reader can reasonably expect to keep.
source: Wikipedia, 'Halley's Comet' -- the 1705 Synopsis of the Astronomy of Comets, the 1531/1607/1682 match, the prediction of a 1758 return, recovery by Johann Georg Palitzsch on 25 December 1758, perihelion 13 March 1759 with a 618-day delay from Jupiter and Saturn, and the Clairaut-Lalande-Lepaute computation landing about a month off at 13 April. Wikipedia, 'Edmond Halley' -- death in January 1742, the 1684 Cambridge visit, his funding of the Principia, and his statement about posterity acknowledging an Englishman.
framing_note: Voice: DISCOVERY + the purest statement of what makes a claim scientific -- it names a date, and the date can betray you. Accuracy rail (the one that matters): Halley did NOT discover the comet; people had recorded it for centuries. What he discovered is that separate sightings were the SAME OBJECT returning -- no rung may say he discovered a comet. Secondary rail: Clairaut's team was about a month off, which is a success, not a miss -- present the near-hit honestly rather than rounding it to 'exactly right'. Dinner-test payoff: T4 (a farmer beat every professional observatory in Europe to it). Distractor mine: comets as omens of a king's death, Aristotle's exhalation theory, Tycho's parallax result, and 'a new comet each time' -- all positions held in earnest. Invitation rung: 2061 is the kid's own appointment with the test. Anti-restatement: the T1 stem gives the three dates and the near-identical orbits and must not contain the words 'one comet returning' before the answer supplies them.
history_overlap: history bank: the 1066 comet on the Bayeux Tapestry and comets-as-omens in medieval chronicles -- this ladder builds no Norman Conquest rung; if the omen theme is used it stays one line inside T5 as the belief the prediction replaced.

name: Cavendish weighs the Earth in a garden shed
scope: Measuring the mass of a planet with two lead balls and a piece of wire. T1: in 1797-98 a fabulously rich and painfully shy English gentleman set out to weigh the entire planet; his laboratory was an outbuilding in his garden at Clapham and his instrument was a six-foot wooden rod hung from a thin wire with a small lead ball at each end -- Henry Cavendish and a torsion balance. T2: the idea was not his -- the geologist and clergyman John Michell designed the apparatus and had it built, then died in 1793 without ever using it, and it reached Cavendish secondhand; he kept Michell's design. T3: MECHANISM -- two twelve-inch lead spheres of about 158 kg each were swung close to the two two-inch, 0.73 kg balls on the rod. Their mutual gravity twisted the wire, moving the rod's ends about a sixth of an inch. The whole trick is that a thin wire resists twisting so feebly that a force far too weak to feel becomes a visible swing you can measure. T4: the paranoia that made it work -- Cavendish sealed the balance in a mahogany case inside a closed shed and observed it through TELESCOPES from OUTSIDE, through holes in the wall, so that his own body heat and breath could not stir a current of air inside. Controlling the experimenter is part of the experiment. T5: the result and what it told us -- Earth's mean density came out at 5.448 times that of water, against the modern figure of 5.514; he was within about one per cent on the first attempt and nobody improved on him for a century. And because the rocks at the surface are only about two and a half times water, the inside had to be far denser -- the first physical evidence that the Earth has a heavy metallic core. Further rungs: he was not chasing the gravitational constant G, which was not even defined until some seventy-five years later -- he reported a density and called it weighing the world; and the earlier rival attempt, the 1774 Schiehallion experiment, which tried to get the same number by measuring how much a Scottish mountain deflected a plumb line.
source: Wikipedia, 'Cavendish experiment' -- 1797-98, Michell's design and his death in 1793, the six-foot rod with 0.73 kg two-inch lead balls, the 158 kg twelve-inch spheres at 225 mm, the roughly 0.16-inch deflection, the mahogany case inside a closed shed with observation by telescope from outside, the result of 5.448 +/- 0.033 times water against a modern 5.514 g/cm3, and the point that Cavendish expressed a density rather than measuring G.
framing_note: Voice: MECHANISM plus method -- the rung about watching through the shed wall is the one that teaches what an experimenter's real enemy is. Accuracy rail (the one that matters): Michell BUILT it and Cavendish RAN it -- credit both; and Cavendish reported Earth's DENSITY, not the gravitational constant, so no rung may say he set out to measure G. Dinner-test payoff: T4 (he would not go in the room in case he breathed on the planet). Distractor mine: the Schiehallion mountain-deflection experiment (a genuine earlier attempt at the same number), plumb-line and pendulum-timing methods, and 'he estimated it from the rocks' -- all real adjacent science. Test-it-yourself hook: a torsion fibre is only a thread, and a straw balance hung from a hair visibly swings at a puff of breath, which is the same sensitivity trick at kitchen scale. Anti-restatement: the T3 stem describes the balls and the wire and must never contain the words 'gravitational attraction between the spheres' before the answer names the mechanism. Lane border: the heavy-core conclusion is science's because it is an INFERENCE FROM CAVENDISH'S NUMBER, not a tour of the Earth's layers.

name: Foucault's pendulum: walk in and watch the planet turn
scope: The first time anyone SAW the Earth rotate, and the myth that rides on its coat-tails. T1: in early February 1851 Leon Foucault sent cards to the scientists of Paris inviting them to come and see the Earth turn, in the meridian room of the Paris Observatory -- and what he showed them was a swinging weight on a wire (he had first tried it in his own cellar in January). T2: the spectacle -- in March 1851, under the dome of the Pantheon, he hung a 28 kg brass-coated lead bob on a 67-metre wire, and Parisians queued to watch the swing plane creep round and knock over pegs set in a ring on the floor. T3: MECHANISM, and it is the counter-intuitive one -- the pendulum is not turning. It keeps swinging in the same plane in space; the floor, the building, Paris and the planet rotate underneath it. T4: the latitude rule -- the plane appears to complete a full circle in 24 hours only at the poles; at Paris, near 49 degrees north, it takes about 32 hours, roughly 11 degrees an hour; at the equator it does not turn at all. The rate follows the SINE of your latitude, which means a Foucault pendulum can tell you how far north you are. T5: the corrected misconception -- the same rotating-frame effect (Coriolis) is constantly claimed to make bathtubs and toilets drain the opposite way in the southern hemisphere. It does not: at that scale the effect is swamped. When Ascher Shapiro finally isolated it at MIT in 1962 he needed a two-metre basin, more than a day for the water to go completely still, and most of a twenty-minute drain to see it -- because the Coriolis acceleration there is around three ten-millionths of gravity. Drain shape and leftover swirl beat the Earth every time. Further rung: Foucault built and named the gyroscope the following year, 1852, to show the same fixed-direction behaviour without a swing.
source: Wikipedia, 'Foucault pendulum' -- the February 1851 Paris Observatory meridian demonstration, the Pantheon installation with a 28 kg brass-coated lead bob on a 67 m wire, roughly 11.3 degrees per hour and a full turn in about 32 hours at the Pantheon's latitude, and the sine-of-latitude law. Societe Francaise de Physique ephemeride, '3 fevrier 1851: premiere demonstration de la rotation de la Terre grace au pendule de Foucault' -- the invitation wording and Arago's involvement, and the January cellar trial. Wikipedia, 'Coriolis force' -- the bathtub myth, Shapiro's 1962 MIT experiment with a two-metre basin and 24-hour settling, Trefethen's southern-hemisphere replication, and the Coriolis acceleration being about 3x10^-7 of gravity at that scale.
framing_note: Voice: DISCOVERY plus the sub-strand's cleanest corrected-misconception rung. The wonder to key at T1 is that before 1851 the Earth's rotation was INFERRED from astronomy and had never been shown to a person standing in a room. Accuracy rail (the one that matters): at T5 the effect is REAL but negligible at sink scale -- the rung must say 'far too weak to beat the shape of the drain', never 'Coriolis is a myth', and no distractor may secretly be the truth. Secondary rail: the invitation is documented in French and translates as an invitation to come see the Earth turn -- render it as a translated invitation, do not present an English sentence as Foucault's verbatim wording. Dinner-test payoff: T5 (the toilet claim, which almost every adult at the table believes). Distractor mine: the toilet and bathtub myth, 'the air in the room drags the pendulum round', the old geocentric objections that a rotating Earth would fling things off, and the perfectly real fact that Coriolis DOES steer hurricanes -- adjacent-and-true, which makes it a superb wrong answer for a sink question. Test-it-yourself hook: most large science museums have one and the pegs fall within an hour.
history_overlap: geography bank: Coriolis-driven weather patterns and hurricane rotation -- science owns the pendulum demonstration and the bathtub correction, and this ladder builds NO hurricane-circulation rung; if Coriolis-and-storms appears at all it is one clause inside the T5 distractor discussion.

name: Falling around the world: why astronauts float
scope: The most widely believed wrong answer in physics, corrected. T1: at the International Space Station's altitude of about 400 km, the Earth's gravity is still roughly ninety per cent as strong as it is on your kitchen floor -- so astronauts are not beyond gravity at all. They float because they and the station are FALLING together, and the astronaut, the wall and the floating pen all fall at exactly the same rate, so nothing presses on anything. T2: Newton drew the picture himself -- in A Treatise of the System of the World he imagined a cannon on a mountaintop firing horizontally: slow, and the ball lands nearby; faster, it lands farther; fast enough, and the ground curves away underneath as fast as the ball drops, so it never lands. That is an orbit. T3: the number that makes it work -- to keep missing the Earth you must move sideways at about 7.7 kilometres per second, roughly 17,500 mph, which carries you right around the planet in about ninety minutes; the crew sees sixteen sunrises a day. T4: the same weightlessness at kid scale -- anything in free fall is weightless, which is why your stomach lifts on the first drop of a rollercoaster, why a dropped lift would feel the same, and why NASA's parabolic-flight aircraft (the 'Vomit Comet') gives about twenty-five seconds of true floating per arc. Orbit is simply free fall that never ends. T5: the precise word is MICROGRAVITY, not zero gravity -- gravity in orbit is not zero and it is not even perfectly uniform, since an astronaut's head and feet sit at slightly different distances from Earth (a tidal effect), and there is still enough thin air at 400 km that the station slowly loses altitude and must be reboosted. Further rungs: what would happen if the station simply stopped in place -- it would fall straight down, because the sideways speed is the entire trick; and the conceptual bridge, Einstein's 'happiest thought', that a person in free fall feels no gravity at all, which became the seed of general relativity.
source: Wikipedia, 'Weightlessness' -- weightlessness as free fall rather than absence of gravity, gravitational acceleration of about 9 m/s2 at ISS altitude (roughly 90 per cent of surface gravity), James Oberg's formulation that what is missing is weight rather than gravity, the microgravity terminology and its tidal justification, and parabolic flight giving about 25-30 seconds per manoeuvre since 1959. Wikipedia, 'Newton's cannonball' -- the mountaintop cannon in A Treatise of the System of the World, the sequence from falling back to circular orbit to ellipse to escape, and orbiting as perpetual falling.
framing_note: Voice: CORRECTED MISCONCEPTION as the flagship rung -- this is the highest-value single correction in the sub-strand because most adults get it wrong. Accuracy rail (the one that matters): gravity at ISS altitude is about ninety per cent of surface gravity (roughly 8.9-9.0 m/s2) -- never 'almost none', never 'zero', and the correct term is microgravity. Secondary rail: Newton's cannonball appears in A Treatise of the System of the World, published posthumously in 1728, not in the Principia proper -- attribute it correctly. Dinner-test payoff: T1. Distractor mine: 'they are too far away for gravity to reach', 'space has no gravity', 'their speed cancels gravity out', 'they are outside the atmosphere so there is nothing to weigh them' -- these are the real popular wrong answers, and every one is a live option to a reader who has not been told. Anti-restatement: the T1 stem must describe the SCENE (a pen hanging motionless in the air beside a floating astronaut, 400 km up) and must not contain 'free fall' or 'falling' anywhere before the answer supplies it. Ceiling discipline: the Einstein rung stays a single conceptual sentence -- no relativity lesson here, that lives in the Einstein-tests ladder.

name: The tides: the Moon's grip on the ocean
scope: A mechanism ladder with a rung where the master himself gets it wrong. T1: twice a day in the Bay of Fundy the sea rises and falls by as much as sixteen metres -- five storeys of water, on a published timetable -- and what schedules it is the Moon's gravity. T2: THE PUZZLE that makes the mechanism worth knowing -- if the Moon pulls the ocean toward itself, why is there a high tide on the FAR side of the Earth at the same moment? Because a tide is made by the DIFFERENCE in pull across the whole planet: the near water is pulled hardest, the solid Earth next, the far water least, so the far water is effectively left behind. Two bulges, and the Earth spins through both. T3: even Galileo whiffed -- in his 1632 Dialogue he insisted tides were water sloshing in its basin from the Earth's spin and orbit combined, and dismissed lunar influence as an occult, astrological superstition; worse, he used this wrong theory as his strongest argument that the Earth moves. T4: Newton fixed it in the Principia (1687) -- the same inverse-square law that holds the Moon accounts for the ocean, and the Sun helps: when Sun and Moon line up at new and full Moon you get big SPRING tides, and at the quarters they work against each other and you get small NEAP tides ('spring' here means to leap up, and has nothing to do with the season). T5: the honest complication -- Newton's tidy two-bulge equilibrium picture actually predicts tides under a metre. Real tides reach sixteen because continents and basin shapes make the water slosh and resonate, and it is Pierre-Simon Laplace's dynamic theory of 1775 that underlies your local tide table -- which is why high tide is not simply when the Moon is overhead. Further rung: the measured consequence -- Earth's spin drags the bulge slightly ahead of the Moon, and the bulge's own gravity tugs the Moon forward, so the Moon is receding about 3.8 cm a year and Earth's day is lengthening about 1.7 milliseconds a century; both are measured by bouncing laser pulses off the corner-cube retroreflectors that Apollo crews left standing on the lunar surface.
source: Wikipedia, 'Theory of tides' -- Galileo's rejection of lunar influence and his sloshing-basin theory in the Dialogue, Newton's equilibrium explanation, the two bulges along the Earth-Moon axis, spring and neap tides, and Laplace's 1775 dynamic theory explaining tides of up to about 15 m against equilibrium theory's sub-half-metre prediction. Wikipedia, 'Tidal acceleration' -- lunar recession measured at +38.30 +/- 0.08 mm per year by lunar laser ranging off Apollo retroreflectors, day lengthening of +1.72 +/- 0.03 ms per century, and the lagging-bulge torque mechanism.
framing_note: Voice: MECHANISM, with a superb 'even the master got it wrong' rung that keeps the ladder honest about heroes. Accuracy rail (the one that matters): the far-side bulge comes from the GRADIENT of the Moon's pull across the Earth, not from centrifugal force flinging water outward -- that popular explanation is wrong and must not appear as the correct answer anywhere. Secondary rail: it is Laplace, not Newton, who makes tide tables work; do not let a rung imply Newton solved tides completely. Dinner-test payoff: the recession rung (mirrors still sitting on the Moon, laser pulses, 3.8 cm a year) -- unforgettable, verifiable, and it makes Apollo permanently useful. Distractor mine: Galileo's sloshing theory, centrifugal force, 'the Earth's spin throws the water out', and Kepler's correct instinct about lunar attraction which Galileo mocked -- all historically live. Lane border: GEOGRAPHY owns the Bay of Fundy as a place and the coastal tour of extreme tides; here Fundy is a one-line hook at T1 and the ladder spends itself on the mechanism and the Galileo-Newton-Laplace sequence.
history_overlap: geography bank: the Bay of Fundy and other extreme-tide places as a place tour -- keep Fundy to the T1 hook only, own the mechanism. geography may also carry tidal-range coastlines generally; no coastal-landform rung belongs here.

name: Goddard, the vacuum, and the correction that took forty-nine years
scope: The sub-strand's flagship reversal, doubling as its momentum backbone. T1: on 13 January 1920 the New York Times ran an unsigned editorial, 'A Severe Strain on Credulity', sneering that a physics professor who thought a rocket could reach the Moon 'seems to lack the knowledge ladled out daily in high schools' -- the professor was Robert H. Goddard. T2: the reversal -- on 17 July 1969, the day after Apollo 11 launched, the same paper printed a correction: further investigation and experimentation had confirmed the findings of Isaac Newton in the seventeenth century, it was now definitely established that a rocket can function in a vacuum as well as in an atmosphere, and the Times regretted the error. Forty-nine years. T3: what makes it delicious -- Goddard had ALREADY run the test. Around 1915-16 at Clark University he fired rockets inside an evacuated chamber (and fired a pistol in one too) and showed that thrust not only survived the vacuum but was GREATER there than in air. The editorial was written against an experiment that already existed. T4: MECHANISM -- the editorial's mistake was believing a rocket pushes against the air. It does not; it pushes against its own exhaust. Newton's third law: the rocket shoves gas backwards and the gas shoves the rocket forwards with an equal and opposite force. Air is not the partner, the propellant is -- and air merely gets in the way, which is exactly why thrust went UP in vacuum. T5: the bookkeeping underneath -- momentum is mass times velocity, and the total momentum of rocket plus exhaust stays what it started as, so throwing mass hard one way must move everything else the other way. It is the same reason a rifle recoils into your shoulder, a garden sprinkler spins, and a person on frictionless ice can travel by throwing a boot. Further rungs: 16 March 1926, his aunt Effie's snowy farm at Auburn, Massachusetts -- the world's first liquid-fuel rocket flight, 2.5 seconds, 41 feet high, landing 184 feet away; the 1919 Smithsonian paper 'A Method of Reaching Extreme Altitudes' where he derived rocket propulsion from conservation of momentum, and whose closing suggestion about signalling from the Moon with flash powder is what set the press off; Goddard's chronic tuberculosis from 1913 and the two decades of work he did anyway; and the office-chair test -- sit on castors, throw something heavy, and roll backwards.
source: Grokipedia, 'Robert H. Goddard' (read directly via browser) -- the 13 January 1920 'Topics of the Times' editorial with the 'ladled out daily in high schools' and 'something better than a vacuum against which to react' wording, the 17 July 1969 retraction the day after the Apollo 11 launch quoted in full, the 1919 Smithsonian paper deriving propulsion from conservation of momentum, and the 16 March 1926 Auburn flight at 41 feet, 2.5 seconds, 184 feet, 60 mph. Wikipedia, 'Robert H. Goddard' -- the editorial title 'A Severe Strain on Credulity' and the 1915 Clark University vacuum-chamber demonstration showing performance decreases under atmospheric pressure. Smithsonian Air & Space and NASA Earth Observatory Goddard profiles -- the pistol-in-a-vacuum-chamber and ring-shaped vacuum-tube experiments of 1915-16. Wikipedia, 'Newton's laws of motion' -- the third law's precise statement, the same-body misconception, its link to conservation of momentum, and rocket propulsion by exhaust rather than air.
framing_note: Voice: REVERSAL, and this ladder deliberately carries the third law and momentum so the analytic content sits inside a story instead of in a thin definitional ladder. Accuracy rail (the one that matters): both quotations must appear only in their documented wording -- never invent a sharper line -- and Apollo 11 LAUNCHED on 16 July 1969, so the correction ran the day after the LAUNCH, not after the 20 July landing. Secondary rail: teach momentum as mass times velocity before any rung tests it. Dinner-test payoff: T3 (he had already done the experiment they said was impossible). Distractor mine: 'rockets push against the air', 'you need something to push off', and the genuinely correct adjacent contrast that JET engines DO need air -- an honest, respectable near-miss that makes a first-class wrong answer -- plus Konstantin Tsiolkovsky's independent 1903 rocket equation. Anti-restatement: the T4 stem gives the editorial's claim and the vacuum result and must not contain 'third law' or 'exhaust' before the answer names them. Lane border: HISTORY owns Apollo and the space race as a Cold War narrative; here 1969 appears only as the correction's timestamp.
history_overlap: history bank: Apollo 11 and the space race as a Cold War narrative -- this ladder keys the 1920 editorial, the vacuum test and the third law only, and 1969 appears solely as the date on the correction. No mission-narrative rung.

name: Archimedes and the lever
scope: The most famous boast in physics, and the exact law hiding underneath it. T1: a Greek in Syracuse claimed that if you gave him a place to stand, he could move the Earth -- Archimedes. Rail it in the same breath: the line is attributed to him by Pappus of Alexandria centuries later, and appears nowhere in Archimedes' own surviving writing. T2: the demonstration King Hiero II demanded -- Plutarch reports that Archimedes, using a compound pulley, drew a fully loaded ship out of the water by himself; Athenaeus instead credits him with launching the enormous ship Syracusia. Both accounts are late, they disagree, and parts of each are implausible -- so this is ancient story, not a lab notebook. T3: THE LAW, which is not a story at all -- in On the Equilibrium of Planes he PROVED geometrically that magnitudes balance at distances inversely proportional to their weights. Double the arm and you halve the force needed. T4: MECHANISM and the price -- you never get work for nothing. If you push with a tenth of the force, you must push through ten times the distance. The same bargain runs a crowbar, a wheelbarrow, a pair of scissors, a bottle opener, a block and tackle, a ramp and a gear train: every simple machine trades distance for force, and none of them creates energy. T5: the honest arithmetic on the boast -- with a perfect rigid lever and a fixed fulcrum, shifting the Earth even slightly would mean walking a distance and taking a time so far beyond a human life that the claim is poetry, not engineering. Saying so is a compliment to Archimedes, whose LAW is exactly right even where his slogan is not. Further rung: the kid-replicable version -- a ruler balanced on a pencil with coins on each end; slide the pencil and feel the trade appear in your fingers.
source: Wikipedia, 'Archimedes' -- the 'give me a place to stand' remark as reported by Pappus of Alexandria, the Hiero II ship account attributed to Athenaeus quoting Moschion (the launching of the Syracusia) versus Plutarch's boast-and-challenge version with both containing historically implausible details, and the law of the lever proved in On the Equilibrium of Planes ('magnitudes are in equilibrium at distances reciprocally proportional to their weights').
framing_note: Voice: MECHANISM, with an attribution rail doing real teaching work -- the difference between what an ancient source SAYS and what a surviving proof SHOWS. Accuracy rail (the one that matters): the 'place to stand' quotation is a later attribution by Pappus, and the ship story exists in two incompatible ancient versions -- present both as ancient accounts, never as eyewitness fact, while the law of the lever is presented as exactly what it is, a proof that still holds. Dinner-test payoff: T4 (you buy force with distance, and the receipt always balances). Distractor mine: the other simple machines (pulley, wedge, screw, wheel-and-axle), the Archimedes screw, and the burning-mirrors legend -- a genuine Archimedes claim that modern replication attempts have repeatedly failed, which is both a strong distractor and a second lesson in ancient testimony. Test-it-yourself hook: T5's ruler-and-coins is a sixty-second experiment. Lane border: HISTORY owns the Roman siege of Syracuse and Archimedes' death; this ladder stays on the lever.
history_overlap: history bank: the Roman siege of Syracuse, Archimedes' war machines and his death at a soldier's hands -- this ladder keeps to the lever, the pulley demonstration and the attribution chain, and builds no siege rung.

name: Neptune found with a pen, and the planet that never was
scope: The analytic backbone of the sub-strand: what an anomaly actually means. T1: by the 1840s Uranus would not keep to its predicted timetable. Rather than abandon Newton's law, two mathematicians assumed an unseen planet was tugging on it and calculated WHERE that planet had to be -- Urbain Le Verrier in Paris and, independently and unpublished, John Couch Adams in Cambridge. T2: the moment -- Le Verrier posted his predicted position to Johann Galle in Berlin. On the night of 23-24 September 1846 Galle and his student Heinrich d'Arrest turned the telescope there, compared the field against a newly printed star chart, and d'Arrest announced that a star in the eyepiece was not on the map. Under an hour of searching, and within a degree of the prediction. T3: the near-miss that teaches method -- James Challis at Cambridge had actually RECORDED Neptune on 8 and 12 August 1846 and never noticed, because he had no up-to-date chart to compare his observations against. Having the data is not the same as having the comparison. T4: THE TRAP -- Le Verrier ran the identical play on Mercury, whose perihelion creeps forward by 43 arcseconds per century more than Newton's law allows, and in 1859 proposed another hidden planet, Vulcan, orbiting inside Mercury. A country doctor, Edmond Lescarbault, reported watching it cross the Sun; Le Verrier computed its orbit to a nineteen-day period. Nobody ever found it. Eclipse searches came up empty for fifty years. T5: the resolution -- in 1915 Einstein's general relativity produced Mercury's 43 arcseconds per century out of the curvature of spacetime near the Sun, with no extra planet required. Same anomaly, same method, opposite lesson: this time it was the LAW that needed fixing, not the census of planets, and nothing in advance told anyone which case they were in. Further rungs: the Anglo-French priority fight over Adams's unpublished work, which Adams himself settled by publicly conceding Le Verrier's priority; and the living echo -- the same reasoning is how astronomers infer dark matter from galaxy rotation and how the hunt for a hypothesised Planet Nine proceeds, an honestly open question the bank should not pretend is settled.
source: Wikipedia, 'Discovery of Neptune' -- Le Verrier's 10 November 1845 and 1 June 1846 memoirs and a prediction accurate to within one degree, Adams's calculations completed 18 September 1845, the 23-24 September 1846 observation by Galle and d'Arrest with the Fraunhofer refractor and the new Hora XXI chart, d'Arrest's 'that star is not on the map', Challis's unrecognised 8 and 12 August 1846 observations for want of a current chart, and the priority dispute with Adams's later concession. Wikipedia, 'Vulcan (hypothetical planet)' -- Mercury's 43 arcseconds per century anomaly, Le Verrier's 1859 proposal, Lescarbault's 26 March 1859 claimed transit, the failed eclipse searches through 1908, and Einstein's 1915 account of the anomaly from spacetime curvature.
framing_note: Voice: a CONCEPT ladder built across named cases -- it carries the native T4/T5 ceiling for this whole sub-strand, and its crown rung is a genuine method lesson rather than a fact. Accuracy rail (the one that matters): the anomaly is 43 arcseconds per CENTURY, an almost absurdly small number, and Vulcan was never found and never later explained away as a small asteroid -- it simply does not exist. Secondary rail: Adams's calculation was real but unpublished and unacted-upon; credit both men and say plainly that Le Verrier's was the one that produced the telescope pointing. Dinner-test payoff: the T4-T5 pair (the same trick that discovered a real planet also invented a fake one, and it took Einstein to tell them apart). Distractor mine: Vulcan itself, an undiscovered moon of Uranus, an error in Uranus's assumed mass, solar oblateness (a genuinely proposed explanation for Mercury), and an unknown asteroid belt -- all real rival mechanisms. Anti-restatement: the T1 stem describes only the misbehaving planet and the refusal to discard Newton, and must never say 'an unseen planet's gravity' before the answer names the inference. Ceiling discipline: the Einstein rung keys the RESULT (the number came out right without a new planet) -- no field equations, no tensors.

name: Testing Einstein's gravity
scope: How a theory of gravity gets checked -- including the honest story of a famous test that was thinner than the headlines. T1: in 1919 two British expeditions sailed to a jungle island off West Africa and to northern Brazil to photograph stars during a total solar eclipse. They were not studying the Sun; they were checking whether the Sun BENDS starlight -- Arthur Eddington at Principe and the second team at Sobral, on 29 May 1919. T2: why it had to be an eclipse -- you can only see stars sitting right beside the Sun when the Moon blots the Sun out. Photograph that star field during totality, photograph the same stars months later at night, and compare: if the positions have shifted outward, the Sun bent their light on the way past. T3: the number that made it decisive -- Newtonian gravity applied to light predicts a deflection of about half the Einstein value at the Sun's edge; general relativity predicts about 1.75 arcseconds, exactly twice. One measurement could choose between two theories. The results were announced jointly by the Royal Society and the Royal Astronomical Society on 6 November 1919, and Einstein was world-famous within days. T4: THE HONEST CAVEAT -- the data were marginal. Eddington's Principe plates were fogged by cloud, and Sobral's main telescope images were degraded, so the usable Sobral data came from a smaller backup instrument. Historians argued for decades that Eddington had chosen the plates that suited him; modern re-analysis largely vindicates his choices, but the real confirmation came from later eclipses from 1922 onward and eventually from radio measurements of quasars. Science does not rest on one heroic afternoon, and saying so is not a retreat. T5: MECHANISM at rubber-sheet level -- in Einstein's picture mass does not reach out and pull; it curves spacetime, and everything moves as straight as it can through curved geometry. Light has no mass and is deflected anyway, because it is following the curve. Further rungs: the working relativity experiment in the kid's pocket -- GPS satellite clocks run about 45 microseconds a day fast because gravity is weaker up there and about 7 microseconds a day slow because they are moving, a net drift of roughly 38 microseconds a day, and uncorrected the position fix would wander by kilometres within a day; and the loudest confirmation of all -- on 14 September 2015 the two LIGO detectors, with four-kilometre arms, registered a passing ripple in spacetime from two black holes of about 36 and 29 solar masses merging, about three solar masses of matter converted to wave energy in a fifth of a second, moving the mirrors by roughly a thousandth of the width of a proton, announced on 11 February 2016 -- and the signal rises in pitch, so you can listen to it as a chirp.
source: Wikipedia, 'Eddington experiment' -- the 29 May 1919 eclipse, the Principe and Sobral expeditions, an Einstein prediction near 1.75 arcseconds against roughly half that from Newtonian gravity, cloud at Principe and blurred main-telescope plates at Sobral with usable data from the backup instrument, the 6 November 1919 joint announcement, the later bias controversy and the modern reanalysis, and confirmation by the 1922 and subsequent eclipses. Wikipedia, 'GW150914' -- detection 14 September 2015, announcement 11 February 2016, black holes of about 36 and 29 solar masses forming a remnant near 62, about 3 solar masses radiated, a distance of roughly 1.3-1.4 billion light-years, a signal of about 0.2 s sweeping 35 to 250 Hz, and a displacement of about a thousandth of a proton's width. Wikipedia, 'Vulcan (hypothetical planet)' consulted for the Mercury cross-reference (owned by the Neptune ladder, not duplicated here).
framing_note: Voice: DISCOVERY plus a MYSTERY-grade honesty rung -- T4 is the reason this ladder exists, because the 1919 eclipse is usually told as a clean triumph and it was not. Accuracy rail (the one that matters): the load-bearing fact at T3 is the FACTOR OF TWO between the Newtonian and Einsteinian deflections, not the decimal -- sources differ slightly on the Newtonian value (about 0.87 arcseconds), so a rung must key the doubling, not a contested digit. Secondary rails: never say Einstein 'disproved Newton' -- Newton's law is still what flies spacecraft; GPS is a NET of about 38 microseconds a day (roughly 45 from gravity minus 7 from speed); and LIGO's distance is about 1.3-1.4 billion light-years, so state it as a range. Mercury's 43 arcseconds per century belongs to the Neptune/Vulcan ladder and must NOT be duplicated here. Dinner-test payoff: the GPS rung -- relativity is running in the kid's pocket right now and the map would be useless without it. Distractor mine: the luminiferous ether, the Newtonian half-deflection, 'light has mass so it falls' (a genuinely respectable pre-1915 half-answer), and Mach's principle. Ceiling discipline: curvature stays at rubber-sheet-plus-honest-caveat -- no field equations, no tensors, no metric.
history_overlap: No sister-bank overlap. SIBLING SUB-STRAND RISK inside science itself: any 'modern physics', 'light', or 'space and the cosmos' sub-strand may also claim the 1919 eclipse and LIGO -- coordinate before building so the eclipse expedition and GW150914 are authored ONCE, here, framed as tests of GRAVITY rather than as optics or cosmology.
